paragraphs: Mitya suddenly flushed crimson.
“Surely you don’t take me for such an out-and-out scoundrel as that? You can’t be serious!” he said indignantly. He looked the prosecutor straight in the face, as if he couldn’t believe his ears.
“I assure you I am serious.... Why would you think I’m not?” It was the prosecutor’s turn to be surprised.

“Oh, how low that would have been! Gentlemen, do you know, you’re torturing me! Let me tell you everything, then, so be it. I’ll confess all my infernal wickedness, but only to put you to shame. You’ll be amazed yourselves at the depths of disgrace a jumble of human passions can sink to. You should know that I had that plan myself, the one you just mentioned, prosecutor! Yes, gentlemen, I too have had that thought in my head all this month. I was on the point of deciding to go to Katya—I was mean enough for that. But think of it! To go to her, to tell her about my treachery, and then, for that very treachery, to pay for carrying it out, to beg money from her, from Katya (to beg, do you hear, to beg), and go straight from her to run away with the other woman, her rival, who hated her and insulted her! You must be mad, prosecutor!”

“I’m not mad, but I spoke in haste, without thinking ... about that feminine jealousy ... if there could be jealousy in this case, as you claim ... yes, perhaps there is something of the kind,” said the prosecutor, smiling.

“But that would have been so infamous!” Mitya brought his fist down fiercely on the table. “It would have been filthy beyond anything! Do you know, she might have given me that money? Yes, she would have given it; she’d certainly have given it, to take revenge on me, to satisfy her vengeance, to show her contempt for me. She has an infernal nature too, and she’s a woman of great wrath. I’d have taken the money, oh yes, I’d have taken it, and then for the rest of my life ... oh, God! Forgive me, gentlemen, I’m shouting like this because that thought has been in my mind so recently, only the day before yesterday, that night when I was having all that trouble with Lyagavy, and then all day yesterday, I remember, until that happened ...”
“Until what happened?” put in Nikolay Parfenovitch curiously, but Mitya did not hear.

“I’ve made you a terrible confession,” Mitya concluded gloomily. “You must appreciate it, and what’s more, you must respect it. If you don’t, if it leaves your souls untouched, then you simply have no respect for me, gentlemen, I tell you that, and I’ll die of shame at having confessed it to men like you! Oh, I’ll shoot myself! Yes, I see, I can already see that you don’t believe me. What, you want to write that down too?” he cried in dismay.

“Yes, what you said just now,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch, looking at him in surprise. “That is, that up to the last hour you were still thinking of going to Katerina Ivanovna to beg that sum from her.... I assure you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, that is a very important piece of evidence for us, for the whole case, I mean ... and especially for you, especially important for you.”

“Have mercy, gentlemen!” Mitya threw up his hands. “Don’t write that, at least; have some shame. I’ve torn my heart in two in front of you, and you seize the chance to finger the wounds in both halves.... Oh, my God!”
In despair he hid his face in his hands.

“Don’t upset yourself so, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” the prosecutor said. “Everything that’s written down will be read over to you afterwards, and anything you don’t agree with we’ll change as you like. But now I’ll ask you one small question for the second time. Has no one, absolutely no one, heard from you about that money you sewed up? I must tell you that is almost impossible to believe.”
“No one, no one! I told you so before, or else you haven’t understood a thing! Leave me alone!”

“Very well. This matter is bound to be cleared up, and there’s plenty of time for it. But meanwhile, consider this. We have perhaps a dozen witnesses that you yourself spread it around, and even shouted almost everywhere, about the three thousand you had spent here. Three thousand, not fifteen hundred. And just now too, when you got hold of the money you had yesterday, you gave many people to understand that you had brought three thousand with you.”
“You have not dozens of witnesses but hundreds, two hundred witnesses, two hundred people heard it, thousands heard it!” cried Mitya.
“Well, you see, they all bear witness to it. And the word _all_ means something.”
“It means nothing. I talked rot, and everyone started repeating it.”
“But what need was there for you to ‘talk rot,’ as you call it?”

“The devil knows. Out of bravado, perhaps ... at having wasted so much money.... Or to try to forget the money I had sewn up, perhaps ... yes, that was why ... damn it ... how many times will you ask me that question? Well, I told a fib, and that was that. Once I’d said it, I didn’t care to correct it. Why does a man tell lies sometimes?”

“That’s very hard to decide, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, why a man tells lies,” the prosecutor observed impressively. “Tell me, though, was that ‘amulet,’ as you call it, that you wore on your neck, a big thing?”
“No, not big.”
“How big, for instance?”
“Fold a hundred-rouble note in half, and that would be the size.”
“You’d better show us what’s left of it. You must have it somewhere.”
“Damnation, what nonsense! I don’t know where it is.”
“But excuse me, where and when did you take it off your neck? By your own account, you didn’t go home.”
“On my way from Fenya’s to Perhotin’s, I tore it off my neck and took out the money.”
“In the dark?”
“What did I need a light for? I did it with my fingers in a minute.”
“Without scissors, in the street?”
“In the market-place, I think it was. Why scissors? It was an old rag. It tore in a minute.”
“Where did you put it afterwards?”
“I dropped it there.”
“Where exactly?”
“In the market-place, in the market-place! The devil knows where. What do you want to know for?”
“That’s extremely important, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. It would be material evidence in your favor. How is it you don’t see that? Who helped you sew it up a month ago?”
“No one helped me. I did it myself.”
“Can you sew?”
“A soldier has to know how to sew. It took no skill to do that.”
“Where did you get the material, that is, the rag you sewed the money into?”
“Are you laughing at me?”
“Not at all. And we’re in no mood for laughing, Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”
“I don’t know where I got the rag—somewhere, I suppose.”
“I would have thought you couldn’t have forgotten that?”
“Honestly, I don’t remember. I might have torn a piece off my linen.”
“That’s very interesting. Tomorrow we might find at your lodgings the shirt, or whatever it is, that you tore the rag from. What sort of rag was it, cloth or linen?”
“Goodness only knows what it was. Wait a bit.... I don’t think I tore it off anything. It was a bit of calico.... I think I sewed it up in a cap of my landlady’s.”
“In your landlady’s cap?”
“Yes. I took it from her.”
“How did you get it?”

“Well, I remember once picking up a cap to use as a rag, maybe to wipe my pen on. I took it without asking, because it was a worthless rag. I tore it up, and I took the notes and sewed them into it. I think it was in that very rag that I sewed them. An old piece of calico, washed a thousand times.”
“And you remember that for certain now?”
“I don’t know about for certain. I think it was the cap. But, hang it, what does it matter?”
“In that case your landlady will remember that the cap was lost?”
“No, she won’t. She never missed it. It was an old rag, I tell you, an old rag not worth a farthing.”
“And where did you get the needle and thread?”
“I’ll stop now. I won’t say any more. Enough of it!” said Mitya, finally losing his temper.
“It’s strange that you should have forgotten so completely where you threw the pieces in the market-place.”

“Have the market-place swept tomorrow, and perhaps you’ll find it,” said Mitya, sneering. “Enough, gentlemen, enough!” he decided in an exhausted voice. “I see you don’t believe me! Not for a moment! It’s my fault, not yours. I shouldn’t have been so ready. Why, why did I degrade myself by confessing my secret to you? It’s a joke to you. I can see that in your eyes. You led me into it, prosecutor! Sing a hymn of triumph if you can.... Damn you, you torturers!”

He bowed his head and hid his face in his hands. The lawyers were silent. A minute later he raised his head and looked at them almost blankly. His face now showed complete, hopeless despair, and he sat mute and passive, as though hardly aware of what was happening. Meanwhile they had to finish what they were doing. They had to start examining the witnesses at once. It was already eight o’clock in the morning. The lights had been put out long ago. Mihail Makarovitch and Kalganov, who had been in and out of the room all through the interrogation, had both gone out again. The lawyers too looked very tired. It was a wretched morning. The whole sky was overcast, and the rain poured down in buckets. Mitya stared blankly out of the window.
“May I look out of the window?” he suddenly asked Nikolay Parfenovitch.
“Oh, as much as you like,” the latter replied.

Mitya got up and went to the window.... The rain lashed against its little greenish panes. He could see the muddy road just below the house, and farther off, in the rain and mist, a row of poor, black, dismal huts, looking even blacker and poorer in the rain. Mitya thought of “Phœbus the golden-haired,” and how he had meant to shoot himself at his first ray. “Perhaps it would be even better on a morning like this,” he thought with a smile. Then he suddenly flung his hand downwards and turned to his “torturers.”

“Gentlemen,” he cried, “I see that I’m lost! But what about her? Tell me about her, I beg you. Surely she needn’t be ruined along with me? She’s innocent, you know. She was out of her mind when she cried last night, ‘It’s all my fault!’ She’s done nothing, nothing! I’ve been grieving over her all night as I sat here with you.... Can’t you tell me, won’t you tell me, what you’re going to do with her now?”

“You can set your mind quite at rest on that score, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” the prosecutor answered at once, with obvious eagerness. “So far we have no grounds for troubling the lady in whom you take such an interest. I trust it may stay that way as the case develops.... On the contrary, we’ll do everything in our power in that matter. Set your mind completely at rest.”
“Gentlemen, I thank you. I knew you were honest, straightforward men in spite of everything. You’ve taken a load off my heart.... Well, what are we to do now? I’m ready.”
“Well, we ought to hurry. We must go on to examine the witnesses without delay. That must be done in your presence, and so—”
“Shouldn’t we have some tea first?” Nikolay Parfenovitch put in. “I think we’ve earned it!”

They decided that if tea was ready downstairs (Mihail Makarovitch had no doubt gone down to get some), they would have a glass and then “go on and on,” putting off their proper breakfast until a better opportunity. Tea really was ready below, and was soon brought up. At first Mitya refused the glass that Nikolay Parfenovitch politely offered him, but then he asked for it himself and drank it greedily. He looked amazingly exhausted. With his Herculean strength, you might have supposed that one night of carousing, even with the most violent emotions mixed in, could have had little effect on him. But he felt he could hardly hold his head up, and from time to time everything around him seemed to heave and dance before his eyes. “A little more and I’ll start raving,” he said to himself.
